claims.text: Single-phase solid-solution formation in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles is governed by competition between kinetic trapping during rapid thermal cycling and a thermodynamic drive toward uniform mixing.
A brief intermediate annealing period during cooling provides sufficient atomic diffusion to overcome kinetic barriers.
Intermediate annealing ensures a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Intermediate annealing stabilizes a single-phase structure that is typically FCC.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles typically display phase separation.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles typically display elemental segregation.
Rapidly heated and cooled noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles typically have uncontrolled morphologies.
A sub-melting intermediate annealing step under an inert atmosphere can permit controlled atomic diffusion before final quenching without full coalescence or decomposition.
An intermediate annealing range of approximately 150–300 °C may be suitable, depending on alloy-specific diffusion activation energies.
The relevant structural mediator is the extent of atomic diffusion during annealing, including grain-boundary mobility and interatomic diffusion length.
Greater atomic diffusion during annealing facilitates more uniform elemental mixing.
Intermediate annealing counteracts kinetic trapping of metastable or segregated phases by allowing atomic redistribution.
Atomic redistribution during annealing enables evolution toward a thermodynamically favored single-phase state.
Enhanced diffusion balances chemical mixing enthalpy and atomic-size disparity in a way that promotes single-phase formation.
Annealed nanoparticles will have greater compositional homogeneity than rapidly quenched nanoparticles without an annealing hold.
Annealed nanoparticles will have a higher fraction of a uniform single-phase, typically FCC, crystal structure than the rapid-quench baseline.
Annealed nanoparticles will show less elemental segregation than the rapid-quench baseline.
The hypothesis applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticle systems containing elements such as Au, Ag, Pt, Pd, and Cu when rapid thermal processing produces kinetic trapping.
The proposed regime requires sub-solidus annealing conditions that avoid temperatures causing significant particle coarsening or decomposition.
Failure to reduce phase-separated regions by at least 20% while improving elemental uniformity relative to the rapid-quench control would falsify the proposed mechanism.
